meta.pageTitle: GATE CSE Theory of Computation Previous Year Questions - Solved PYQs

questions.text:
Let [latex]L_{1}=\{w \in \{0,1\}*|w[/latex] has at least as many occurrences of (110)'s as (011)'s}.
Let [latex]L_{2}=\{w \in \{0,1\}*|w[/latex] has at least as many occurrence of (000)'s as (111)'s}.

Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.solution:
L1: 110 and 011 occurrences alternate in a binary string, so their counts differ by at most 1, depending only on how the string starts and ends. A finite automaton can check this [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] regular.

L2: counts of 000 and 111 can grow independently (e.g. [latex]0^n1^n[/latex] type strings), and comparing them needs unbounded counting [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not regular.

Answer: L1 is regular but not L2

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: L1 is regular but not L2
L2 is regular but not L1
Both L1 and L2 are regular
Neither L1 nor L2 are regular

questions.text:
Let [latex]\lt M \gt[/latex] be the encoding of a Turing machine as a string over [latex]\Sigma[/latex]={0,1}.
Let L = { [latex]\lt M \gt[/latex] |M is a Turning machine that accepts a string of length 2014}.
Then, L is
questions.solution:
RE: run M on all strings of length 2014 in parallel (dovetailing) and accept if any one is accepted.

Undecidable: it is a non-trivial property of the language of M, so by Rice's theorem it is undecidable.

Answer: undecidable but recursively enumerable

questions.text: Let [latex]A \leq _{m}B[/latex] denotes that language A is mapping reducible (also known as many-to-one reducible) to language B. Which one of the following is FALSE?
questions.solution:
If [latex]A\le_m B[/latex], A is "no harder" than B. So decidability/RE-ness of B passes down to A, and undecidability of A passes up to B. Options 1, 2, 3 are true.

Option 4 is false: B being non-RE says nothing about A. Example: a decidable language A (non-trivial) reduces to the complement of the halting problem, which is not RE, yet A is RE.

Answer: If [latex]A\le_m B[/latex] and B is not RE then A is not RE

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: If [latex]A\leq _{m}B[/latex] and B is recursive then A is recursive
If [latex]A\leq _{m}B[/latex] and A is undecidable then B is undecidable
If [latex]A\leq _{m}B[/latex] and B is recursively enumerable then A is recursively enumerable.
If [latex]A\leq _{m}B[/latex] and B is not recursively enumerable then A is not recursively enumerable

questions.text:
If [latex]L_{1}=\{a^{n}|n\geq 0\}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}=\{b^{n}|n\geq 0 \}[/latex], Consider
(I) [latex] L_{1}\cdot L_{2}[/latex] is a regular language
(II) [latex] L_{1} \cdot L_{2}= \{a^{n}b^{n}|n \geq 0\}[/latex]
Which one of the following is CORRECT?
questions.solution:
[latex]L_1\cdot L_2=\{a^mb^n\mid m,n\ge0\}=a^*b^*[/latex], which is regular [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (I) true.

The counts of a and b are independent, so it is not [latex]\{a^nb^n\}[/latex] (e.g. aab is in it) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (II) false.

Answer: Only (I)

questions.text:
Which of the regular expressions given below represent the following DFA?

I) 0*1(1+00*1)*
II) 0*1*1+11*0*1
III) (0+1)*1
questions.solution:
The DFA accepts exactly the strings that end with 1: III [latex](0+1)^*1[/latex] True. I [latex]0^*1(1+00^*1)^*[/latex] also describes "ends with 1" True.

II misses strings like 0101 (it allows no 0 after a 1 unless the string starts with 1).

Answer: I and III only
